meta.title: Choosing an Agent Framework
meta.thesis: Choosing an Agent Framework is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A platform team compares frameworks for a customer-support agent with tools, memory, and approvals. By the end, they should be able to build or review agent-framework selection matrix and proof-of-concept plan, measure framework fit against durability, observability, and deployment needs, and catch the failure where the team picks a popular framework that cannot express its control flow.

mentalMap.title: Choosing an Agent Framework: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Choose an agent framework by the control problem: integration layer, explicit graph, data-centric RAG, provider-native runtime, role teams, or enterprise ecosystem.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: The right framework is the one whose native abstraction matches the product risk and workflow shape.

modules.title: Start with the hardest product constraint
modules.sub: Framework choice follows the risk, not the logo.
modules.summary: A framework should make the hard part easier.
objectives: Identify the core constraint in an agent app.
Choose a framework based on native abstraction.

blocks.title: The bottleneck chooses the framework

spans.text: Problem anchor: a support triage app needs tool calls, customer data retrieval, human approval for refunds, and trace review. The best framework depends on which part is hardest: integration, RAG, explicit state, provider-native handoffs, or enterprise deployment.
A framework is not a quality guarantee. It gives you defaults and vocabulary. You still own security, evals, cost, and product behavior.
Write one sentence: “The hardest part of this app is...” before naming a framework.

blocks.analogy: Choose the wrench for the bolt, not the shiniest toolbox.

spans.text: If the hardest part is broad provider/tool integrations, LangChain may fit. If the hard part is approval and resumable state, LangGraph or a workflow engine matters. If the hard part is private data indexing, LlamaIndex is stronger.
If the app is OpenAI-native with handoffs and tracing, OpenAI Agents SDK may be faster. If the org is Microsoft/Azure-heavy, Microsoft Agent Framework may fit better.

items.text: Write the product workflow and failure modes.
Mark state, data, tools, approvals, observability, and deployment needs.
Compare frameworks on the hardest two needs.
Prototype the riskiest path before committing.

blocks.title: Selection anchor
blocks.prompt: What should you identify before choosing an agent framework?

options.text: The framework with the longest README.
The hardest product constraint or failure mode the framework must own.
The one with the most agent personas by default.

blocks.explanation: Framework fit starts with the problem shape.

modules.title: Match abstraction to workflow shape
modules.sub: Integration layers, graphs, data engines, and teams solve different problems.
modules.summary: The native object tells you what the framework is good at.
objectives: Compare LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Microsoft stack.
Name each framework’s center of gravity.

blocks.title: Look at the native nouns

spans.text: LangChain centers models, tools, prompts, middleware, and integration breadth. LangGraph centers state graphs, nodes, edges, checkpoints, and interrupts. LlamaIndex centers documents, nodes, indexes, retrievers, query engines, agents, and workflows.

CrewAI centers agents, tasks, crews, and flows. OpenAI Agents SDK centers agents, runs, tools, handoffs, sessions, guardrails, and tracing. Microsoft stack centers kernels/plugins historically and newer Agent Framework workflows, middleware, telemetry, and Azure integration.
If your design diagram uses the framework’s native nouns naturally, fit is probably improving.

blocks.analogy: A framework’s nouns reveal its worldview.

cells.text: State graph with checkpoints and interrupts.
Control flow, resume, approval, branches matter.
You own graph design and tests.
Agents still need tool and citation eval.

blocks.title: Native nouns
blocks.prompt: Which framework naturally centers nodes, edges, checkpoints, and interrupts?
blocks.explanation: Those are LangGraph’s core orchestration concepts.

modules.title: State, durability, and human review narrow the field
modules.sub: Control-flow requirements often decide the runtime.
modules.summary: State needs are often more decisive than model choice.
objectives: Compare thread state, graph checkpoints, workflow durability, and sessions.
Choose explicit graphs when branches matter.
Recognize when a workflow engine belongs underneath.

blocks.title: State is where demos become products

spans.text: If the agent only answers one question, a provider SDK or simple chain may be enough. If it branches, waits for review, resumes after interruption, or must survive deploys, state control becomes central.

LangGraph gives graph checkpoints and interrupts. OpenAI Agents SDK offers sessions and continuation strategies. Durable engines such as Temporal/Inngest/Restate may sit underneath when external orchestration spans long periods.
Draw the resume point after a crash. If you cannot, your framework plan is incomplete.

blocks.analogy: State is the bookmark in a long task.

spans.text: A refund agent retrieves policy, drafts a recommendation, pauses for human approval, then updates a ticket. LangGraph handles explicit pause/resume well. A durable workflow engine may wrap it if the approval can wait days.
A one-turn FAQ agent does not need that machinery.

items.text: Test resume and cancellation before release.

blocks.title: State criterion
blocks.prompt: Which need points most strongly toward LangGraph or a workflow engine?

options.text: The answer should use a friendly tone.
The agent must pause for approval and resume after a process restart.
The UI needs a blue button.

blocks.explanation: Pause/resume is a control-flow and durability requirement.

modules.title: Prototype the riskiest slice, not the happiest path
modules.sub: A framework comparison should test the failure mode.
modules.summary: The right prototype attacks the scary part first.
objectives: Choose evaluation tasks for framework fit.

blocks.title: Framework evaluation is a product experiment

spans.text: Prototype the slice that could fail expensively: approval resume, citation support, tool permission, query-engine retrieval, or handoff ownership. Do not choose based on how quickly a hello-world agent runs.
Spaced recall: from multi-agent orchestration, compare against a simpler baseline. Framework complexity must earn its place.
The prototype should make one framework advantage or weakness observable.

blocks.title: Tiny framework fit helper
blocks.explanation: The helper is not a universal truth; it forces the learner to map needs to native framework strengths.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict the two printed recommendations.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints LlamaIndex for data/query-engine needs and LangGraph for explicit graph plus interrupts.

blocks.title: Prototype target
blocks.prompt: What should a framework prototype test first?

options.text: The riskiest product constraint, such as resume, retrieval quality, tool policy, or handoff ownership.
Only whether the logo appears in docs.

blocks.explanation: Framework fit is about the hard production path.

modules.title: Plan migration, observability, and lock-in
modules.sub: The selection decision continues after the prototype.
modules.summary: A framework choice is an operating decision.
objectives: Name provider or ecosystem lock-in tradeoffs.

spans.text: Ask how traces work, where prompts and tool outputs are logged, how evals run, how versions are pinned, how deployment works, and what happens if the provider or package changes.

Provider-native frameworks can be faster inside one ecosystem; provider-neutral frameworks can reduce lock-in but add integration work. Enterprise stacks can solve identity and hosting while constraining portability.
Include an exit or migration note in the design review.
Use this checklist before committing a product team.

items.text: The chosen framework owns the hardest product constraint better than alternatives.
A thin prototype exercises the risky path, not only a demo.
State, memory, approvals, and durability have explicit ownership.
Tool security, evals, and tracing are planned outside model prompts.
Versioning, provider coupling, deployment, and migration risks are documented.

blocks.title: Selection review
blocks.prompt: What is a red flag in a framework decision?

options.text: Running a prototype with real eval cases.
Choosing the framework before naming the workflow’s hardest failure mode.

blocks.explanation: A framework should be selected to solve a named problem.
